title: Salutation to the armed One
hookLine: namo sastr paane: salutation to the One with weapons in hand, the protector (Jaap)
tomorrow: Sun of suns, moon of moons

cards: A lifeguard's whistle. A crossing guard's raised hand and bright vest. A parent stepping, without thinking, between a child and a dog that's barking too hard.
Protection doesn't always look gentle. Sometimes it's loud, and fast, and holding something: a rescue tube, a stop sign. The people who stand between us and harm are rarely remembered as soft.
They're remembered as there. Jaap Sahib has a line for the One who stands there.

teach.h: SASTR: A WEAPON HELD IN THE HAND.
teach.b: Among the salutations comes namo sastr paane. Namo, a bow. Sastr, or shastar, is a weapon held in the hand, like a sword.
Paan is the hand. Salutation to the One with weapons in hand. The next words add astr, a weapon that's thrown or shot, like an arrow: the One honored with that weapon too.
Right after aroop and ajooni, it can startle.

teach.h: WHY DOES THE FORMLESS NEED A SWORD?
teach.b: Why would the formless need a sword?
Because for the Tenth Guru, the sword is a picture of protection. He lived in violent years. His father, Guru Tegh Bahadur, was executed in Delhi.
The Guru himself fought battles to defend his people, and in his Persian letter, the Zafarnama, he speaks of the four sons he lost.
In that letter he wrote, in effect, that when every other way has failed, it is right to take up the sword. Not first. Last.
So the weapon in the One's hand isn't a threat to the innocent; it's the arm that defends them. The idea runs through Sikh life.
The Ardas, the prayer said at the close of Sikh gatherings, begins by remembering Bhagauti, a name for the Divine as sword and power.
Amritdhari Sikhs carry the kirpan, a small sword, as an article of faith, a promise to protect, not a tool for picking fights.
And the ideal has a name you met last year: sant sipahi, the saint-soldier.
Gentle in the heart, ready in the hands. Jaap bows to the One who is both.

how: Amritdhari Sikhs carry the kirpan as an article of faith tied to protecting others, and the Ardas said at the close of Sikh gatherings opens by remembering Bhagauti, the Divine as sword and power.

games.q: you're the Tenth Guru, and every peaceful way of protecting your people has failed. what does the Zafarnama say?
o: it is then right to take up the sword.
games.why: the letter says the sword is lawful only when all other means have failed: the sword comes last.

practice: Picture someone who protects you, or once did, a parent, a teacher, a nurse, a stranger who stepped in, and the moment they stood between you and harm.
Breathe in and remember what that safety was like; breathe out, thank them silently, and wonder, gently, who you might stand in front of. If you pray, you can say namo sastr paane.

wordCard.voice: Shastar. A weapon held in the hand — namo sastr paane, Jaap's bow to the One with weapons in hand, the protector who defends the weak.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: shastar, a weapon held in the hand; Jaap writes it sastr, in namo sastr paane.

carryVoice: Your line: the protector. The sword comes last, and it's there to defend. Day three hundred forty-one.
